title: What are we building?
points: A title and its image form one example
Predict one of six benchmark labels
whatif: A prediction is not independent fact-checking.
narration: Our UROP project studies multimodal fake news classification. Multimodal simply means using more than one kind of input: here, a short post title and its associated image. A model learns patterns from labelled examples and predicts one of six categories. It does not search the internet or independently prove whether a claim is true. This video builds from those basics to the actual architecture, decisions, results, and failure cases.

title: Understand the six classes
points: True · Satire/Parody · Misleading Content
Imposter · False Connection · Manipulated
whatif: These are weak benchmark labels, not verified truth certificates.
narration: The six labels are True, Satire or Parody, Misleading Content, Imposter Content, False Connection, and Manipulated Content. False Connection concerns a mismatch between text and image. Manipulated Content includes edited images. In Fakeddit, labels largely come from the source community rather than independent verification of every post. A system can therefore learn community style and dataset shortcuts. High benchmark accuracy does not automatically make it a reliable real world fact checker.

title: The faculty dataset and lineage
points: 563,601 train · 59,299 validation · 59,270 test
682,170 usable pairs; official split membership retained
whatif: Exactly 491 decode failures excluded with approval; no new splits.
narration: We used the faculty linked Fakeddit release with three files: multimodal train, multimodal validate, and multimodal test public. The original files contain six hundred eighty two thousand six hundred sixty one rows. Exactly four hundred ninety one images failed strict decoding and were excluded with approval, before model results were used. The usable counts are on screen. Original files, identities, titles, six labels, and split assignments were preserved. We did not manually create replacement splits.

title: Train, validate, then test
points: Train learns weights; validation selects the checkpoint
Held-out test evaluates one frozen selection
whatif: Skipping validation or tuning on test makes the reported result misleading.
narration: Training data teaches the model. Validation data compares checkpoints without updating their weights. The held out test is reserved for the final frozen choice. If we repeatedly change a model after seeing its test result, that test stops being an honest final examination. Separate post identities do not guarantee independent images: our audit found cross split byte identical image groups. That is a remaining leakage and comparability risk, not something to hide.

title: Turn titles into model inputs
points: WordPiece token IDs + attention mask
Maximum 128 tokens; batch padding
whatif: Removing the mask can make padding affect the representation.
narration: A computer cannot feed raw words directly into BERT. Its WordPiece tokenizer converts a title into integer token identifiers. An attention mask identifies real tokens and padding. We cap inputs at one hundred twenty eight tokens, then pad each batch. BERT uses attention to relate words to their context. Its special classification token produces a seven hundred sixty eight dimensional representation. Changing tokenization or truncation changes the experiment and must be registered and checked.

title: Prepare images consistently
points: RGB · deterministic training crop · 224 × 224
Evaluation: resize to 232, center-crop to 224
whatif: Skipping normalization shifts inputs away from the pretrained model's expectations.
narration: Images are decoded, converted to red, green, and blue channels, and normalized using the expected ImageNet channel statistics. Training uses a reproducible random resized crop, linked to the seed, epoch, and example identity. Evaluation resizes the shorter side to two hundred thirty two, then center crops to two hundred twenty four pixels. These rules prevent arbitrary evaluation changes. Skipping normalization or using a different crop can shift the input distribution and change predictions.

title: Two pretrained encoders
points: BERT-base: 768 features; selected text epoch-4 initialization
ResNet-50: 2,048 pooled features; ImageNet V2 initialization
whatif: Both encoders were fine-tuned; neither was frozen in this experiment.
narration: The text encoder is BERT base uncased, initialized from our verified selected text only checkpoint. The image encoder is ResNet fifty, initialized with ImageNet version two weights. ResNet uses residual connections to help information and gradients flow through a deep network. We remove its original image classifier and keep two thousand forty eight pooled features. Both encoders and the fusion head are fine tuned. Starting from useful pretrained representations reduces the burden compared with learning everything from random weights.

title: Make the feature sizes compatible
points: Text: 768 → 512 + LayerNorm
Image: 2,048 → 512 + LayerNorm
whatif: Without compatible projections, elementwise maximum has a shape mismatch.
narration: The two encoders produce different sized vectors. Separate learned linear projections map each to five hundred twelve dimensions. Layer normalization helps control feature scale. These projections are learned adapters, not manually defined semantic coordinates. Without matching sizes, elementwise maximum cannot combine the vectors. Removing normalization or changing the projection size would be a different architecture requiring new training and validation. We did not run an ablation proving this size is universally optimal.

title: What maximum fusion really does
points: Take the larger value at each feature position
whatif: It does not select one entire modality, or average class probabilities.
narration: Maximum fusion compares the two projected values at every position and keeps the larger one. The small example on screen illustrates the operation; the real vectors have five hundred twelve positions. Some positions can come from text and others from the image. This is not voting between class predictions. Addition changes the combined scale. Concatenation creates a larger vector and needs a compatible head. Those are legitimate alternatives, but comparing them requires separately controlled experiments.

title: From fused features to six probabilities
points: 512 → 256 → GELU → dropout 0.2 → 6 logits
Softmax converts logits to probabilities
whatif: Dropping a branch changes the model; retrain rather than reuse it blindly.
narration: The fused vector enters a linear layer with two hundred fifty six outputs, a GELU activation, dropout with probability zero point two, and a final layer producing six scores called logits. GELU adds nonlinearity. Dropout discourages dependence on particular activations during training and is off during evaluation. For training, cross entropy takes the raw logits directly. For reporting predictions, softmax converts logits into six probabilities that sum to one. The largest probability gives the predicted label. The network has about one hundred thirty four million trainable parameters.

title: How learning changes the weights
points: Cross-entropy measures error; backpropagation computes gradients
AdamW updates both encoders and the classifier
whatif: Without updates, validation is measurement—not training.
narration: Cross entropy penalizes the model when it gives too little probability to the correct training label. Backpropagation calculates how weights contributed to that loss. Adam W updates the parameters, with weight decay for regularization. The learning rates differ: BERT uses one times ten to the minus five, the image encoder one times ten to the minus four, and the head one times ten to the minus three. A warmup and decay scheduler controls their evolution.

title: Fit the experiment onto a T4
points: Microbatch 8 × accumulation 4 = effective batch 32
FP16 autocast, gradient scaler and clipping at 1
whatif: A batch-size change can alter optimization; it is not just a speed switch.
narration: We used one Tesla T four cloud GPU in Kaggle, even when two devices were allocated. Eight examples fit into each microbatch. Accumulating gradients over four microbatches produces an effective batch of thirty two before an optimizer boundary. Mixed precision saves memory, a gradient scaler helps handle numerical range, and gradient clipping limits extreme updates. These details affect learning and recovery. Changing batch size or the schedule midway would break the controlled continuation.

title: Four epochs, four validations, one test
points: An epoch is one full pass over the training split
Select highest validation Macro-F1, then lower loss, then earlier epoch
whatif: Four epochs are one seed-42 experiment—not four independent replications.
narration: One epoch is a complete pass over the training set. Our registered budget was four epochs, each followed by a full validation. The selection rule was highest validation macro F one, then lower loss, then earlier epoch if still tied. An early stopping rule existed, but this run completed all four epochs. Training interruptions were resumed within the same experiment. After validation selection was frozen, we ran one full final test. Independent metric recomputation is not an additional model test.

title: Which checkpoint won—and why?
points: Epoch 3: highest accuracy, 88.5344%
Epoch 4: highest Macro-F1, 0.829303 → selected
whatif: Epoch 4's loss worsened; it did not improve every measure.
narration: Epoch three had the highest validation accuracy, eighty eight point five three four four percent. Epoch four had the highest macro F one, zero point eight two nine three zero three, so epoch four won under the declared rule. Its validation accuracy was slightly lower, and its loss was higher. Better class decisions can coexist with worse confidence on mistakes. We retained that tradeoff rather than changing the rule after seeing results or picking whichever checkpoint looked best on the test.

title: Read the final metrics correctly
points: Test: 88.1458% accuracy · Macro-F1 0.826415
Imposter Content remains weakest: test F1 0.662188
whatif: Accuracy alone can conceal weaker minority classes.
narration: Final test accuracy was eighty eight point one four five eight percent, and macro F one was zero point eight two six four one five. Accuracy measures the fraction correct. Micro F one equals accuracy in this exhaustive single label task. Precision asks how many predicted class items were correct. Recall asks how many actual class items were found. F one balances precision and recall. Macro F one weights classes equally; weighted F one uses class frequency. Balanced accuracy averages class recalls. Cross entropy also evaluates confidence. Imposter Content remained the weakest class by test F one. Confusion matrices show which classes were mistaken for each other.

title: What does the paper comparison prove?
points: Paper: 86.00% validation / 85.88% test
Our selected model: 88.5074% / 88.1458%
whatif: +2.2658 test percentage points is a numerical comparison, not controlled superiority.
narration: The matching paper reference is six way BERT plus ResNet fifty with maximum fusion. Our test accuracy is two point two six five eight percentage points higher, exceeding the numerical one point aspiration. However, the paper used a different feature and training pipeline. Our available image cohort excludes decoding failures, and we used extra text warm start training. One seed, cross split image duplication, and the unresolved paper versus release row count difference limit the claim. Comparable paper F one and loss values were not reported.

title: Why preparation and recovery mattered
points: Image audit → lossless packed reader → cloud GPU → private outputs
Save model, optimizer, scheduler, scaler, RNG, cursor and selection history
whatif: Weights alone cannot reproduce the exact interrupted training trajectory.
narration: Preparation took time because image decoding, storage, transfers, and slow loading had to be resolved before trustworthy training. We preserved original image bytes, verified packed inputs, and used a cached archive reader on the cloud runtime. Recovery saved not just weights, but optimizer, scheduler, scaler, random states, sample cursor, crop rules, and selection history. A spinner or old notebook output is not proof of activity. Fresh counters, timestamps, saved outputs, checksums, and independent prediction checks establish what actually completed.

title: Defend the design—and know what is next
points: BERT + ResNet-50 is a paper-aligned baseline, not the newest possible model
Text-only complete · text + image complete · image-only pending
whatif: Use a new registered experiment for newer models, ablations or different data.
narration: Why these models? They give a recognizable paper aligned baseline, useful pretrained features, and a feasible T four implementation. We did not prove they beat every newer alternative. CLIP, vision transformers, and newer text encoders are possible future studies, not completed experiments. Removing images, changing fusion, or freezing an encoder requires retraining and validation. Skipping the held out test removes our final performance check. Next is the image only baseline, followed by controlled ablations and repeated seeds if approved. You now have the pipeline, its rationale, its evidence, and its limits.
